speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We live in a world of greater uncertainty and faster change today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Last month, I attended the Group of 20 (G20) Labour and Employment Ministerial Meeting, and the mood was one of concern.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Unemployment at 5.8% has barely fallen from the peak of the crisis of 6%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Labour force participation is also lower than before the crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Back home, our economy and workforce are in transition, too.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Our workforce is ageing at one of the fastest rates in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Importantly, each generation of Singaporeans is aspiring to do better, with better education, better jobs and better incomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: To avoid ending up with the challenges that many countries are now facing of high youth unemployment, sticky unemployment and declining labour force participation, we must get three things right.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: First, we need to quicken the transformation of industry, to make every job a better job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry and sector agencies are leading this effort to create the new industries, new businesses, and new jobs of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, we will need to quicken the transformation of the workforce, to make every worker a better worker.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) is leading the effort to inculcate lifelong learning, from pre-employment education to professional and continuing education.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If workforce transformation lags behind industry transformation, workers will miss the opportunities for better jobs while businesses will not have the manpower they need.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We would end up with higher structural unemployment and an over-reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: On the other hand, if industry transformation lags behind workforce transformation, there will be a shortage of quality jobs for our people, leading to higher under-employment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Therefore, the third thing we must do right is to match every better worker to every better job, and make every career a better career for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 29 Clauses 9 and 10 of the Bill provide for the functions and powers of WSG.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: I will now outline three key areas WSG will strive to do more and do better for our workers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: First, for our workers, WSG will not only help individuals find jobs but also help them build careers at all life stages.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Lifelong career conversion will become more widespread in the future economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Holding a single job or career through life will become less common.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: The new reality is that workers may need not only to switch between jobs and employers, but also between types of industries and modes of employment, be it traditional or emerging.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, the Wokforce Development Agency (WDA), Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) and partners are actively helping jobseekers to find jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: At the same time, WSG will do more to help them manage their career transitions throughout their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Second, at the workforce level, WSG will strengthen the inclusiveness of our local workforce in the face of disruptive change.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Today, WDA serves many in the workforce, be it young or old workers, professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) or non-PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: It has also built up partnerships to support special worker segments, such as with SG Enable to support the hiring of persons with disabilities, and with the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises (SCORE) and the Industrial and Services Co-operative Society (ISCOS) to help ex-offenders return to work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But we recognise that disruptive technology and innovation will bring not just new opportunities, but new threats, too, to all groups of workers, including PMETs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: If we are not proactive, there is a danger that some will be displaced and made redundant by technology, and our workforce may become less inclusive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: WSG will, therefore, reach out to help every segment of workers, to adapt and upgrade with technology, so that we can all benefit and be part of the transformation of our economy and workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Third, at the industry and company levels, WSG will help businesses create better quality jobs to attract and build a stronger Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: This is a key priority for firms as workforce growth will slow and competition for manpower will only become keener.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: WSG will support companies to adopt new business models, be more manpower-lean and create progressive workplaces to fully utilise the skills and talent of our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: So, whether you are in your 20s looking for your first job, or in your 30s looking for your next job, or in your 40s or 50s looking for your next career, or in your 60s or beyond looking to make your next contribution, WSG can support you.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Industry and businesses can, likewise, expect WSG to be employer-centric, helping them to develop their manpower pipeline, sector by sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Working in partnership, WSG and the sector agencies and tripartite partners are developing industry manpower plans under the respective Industry Transformation Maps.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: These plans will articulate the jobs and careers we strive to create in the future, for us to help match workers – both new job entrants and mid-careerists – to these jobs and career opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Page: 30 Last, but not least, WSG will leverage new technology and platforms to widen the reach and impact of its services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Unions, employers and the Government are partnering one another through a constructive spirit of trust and mutual alignment to support our workers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Partnership will be a key feature in all of WSG's work.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Within the Government, it will partner economic agencies on industry transformation, and with MOE and SSG on lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Across each industry, WSG will work with employers, business chambers and trade associations, and unions to deepen ties and achieve win-win outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: In employment facilitation, it will partner best-in-class employment agencies to help workers secure better jobs, and technology providers to expand its effectiveness and reach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: But the most important partner will be the workers of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: We need every individual to play his or her part to adapt and grow in this new environment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: With a dedicated agency in WSG and the collective endeavours of all our partners, I am confident that we can do more than before to match the aspirations of our people and the needs of our businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Mr Lim Swee Say)
text: Together, we can make sure that the innovative growth of the economy is also inclusive growth for our people.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I rise in support of the Workforce Development Agency (Amendment) Bill which reorganises WDA as WSG for short and refocuses its functions and duties in relation to SSG.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I am glad to note that WSG's central mission is to enable Singaporeans to have quality jobs and careers and that it will ensure that industry, skills and jobs are transformed in sync.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I particularly laud the fact that WSG will work towards ensuring locals remain in employment through the provision of employment facilitation and career services.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The work of the new WSG is extremely crucial as Singapore enters into this period of economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The situation is further aggravated by the fact that we have cyclical forces, structural forces as well as economic restructuring and transformation all in one go.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The silver lining is that we have a tight labour market situation, foreign manpower is being contained and unemployment is relatively low compared to many other developed countries.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Page: 31 Likewise, job creation continues as we see more than 60,000 jobs posted on the National Jobs Bank alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Despite the large number of job postings, especially of professionals, managers and executives (PME) positions, one key trend, however, is the rise in the number of PMEs being affected by both cyclical and structural unemployment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At our National Trade Union Congress' (NTUC's) U PME Centre as well as e2i, we have also seen a surge in the past year in the number of PMEs coming to us to seek help, especially in the area of finding job placements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This year, I foresee that figure to stay high if not higher than last year, as the industries, sectors and positions affected by layoffs are mostly PMET ones.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the rapidly ageing workforce, I am particularly worried for those who are above 40 years of age as they take a much longer time to find employment and are more vulnerable to layoffs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I, therefore, submit that WSG should do more and do even better to help PMEs, particularly those above age 40, to connect them to good jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I submit that WSG needs to find ways to address and overcome three mismatches.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They are the mismatch of skills, the mismatch of jobs and the mismatch of expectations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Despite many jobs posted on the National Jobs Bank, most jobs posted require some form of experience, skillset or expertise and, therefore, many Singaporeans may not fit the bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Local PMEs may lack the requisite skills and experience and, possibly, the regional and international experience.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This contributes to the structural challenge that we face as a country and I foresee we will face in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: My colleagues at our U PME Centre and e2i have highlighted that there are some PMEs who go to them with unrealistic expectations in terms of the type of jobs and conditions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Then, I also hear of employers who lament and do not hire mature PMEs because they claim many of them cannot change, they cannot adapt to the new requirements expected of them, and a host of other ageist remarks.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are also companies which do not take proactive steps to redesign, recreate or resize the jobs or manage the change.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our society, too, must recognise and expect that we have a growing ageing workforce and that there will be an ever increasing number of PMEs, especially mature ones, in our midst.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are cases where PMEs are not well-matched with their current jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: They do jobs which they have neither passion nor interest for.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Sometimes, the job size is too small or the quality of the job is not good.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: There are those whose characters or personalities do not quite fit or match the kind of requirements the job entails.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Then again, there are those who are over-skilled or over-qualified for the jobs, resulting in an underemployment situation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With WSG, I have three suggestions for it to do more and do better.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, I am particularly glad that many Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs) have been rolled out under Adapt and Grow but I feel the Adapt and Grow programme also needs to adapt and grow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: PCPs will have to be even more responsive, relevant and flexible across more sectors and more PME jobs because new jobs are created in new areas daily and we have what we call the "3G" jobs; jobs which are going, going, gone on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We can and should mount greater efforts, dedicate more resources and do even better in facilitating, connecting and placing PMEs into good jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I urge more employers to step forward to partner our sectoral committees to offer even more PCPs in this tight labour market situation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I suggest we strengthen our outreach of CSP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides wage support, emotional support of unemployed PMEs is also vital.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We have expanded and extended this programme so as to confront the structural unemployment challenge.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We look forward to WSG as well as potential employers partnering us in our journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The desired outcome is one where the potential of every worker is fully realised and maximised.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   With economic uncertainty and a weak global demand, retrenchment among Singapore's PMEs will rise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The situation is aggravated by unemployment caused by cyclical and structural forces as well as economic transformation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope the new WSG can pay attention to three areas.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, WSG should put in more resources to help PMEs to find a job that can maximise their potential.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: We should also strengthen the outreach of the CSP so that more employers and employees can benefit.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: (In English): In conclusion, with the new WSG, we can and should use this opportunity to do more and do better to develop what I call the "Gen R" worker, one who is ready, relevant and resilient: Ready with new Skills, Relevant for new Jobs and Resilient to new changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The establishment of WSG is timely, as the Minister has correctly put it, as the Government tries to steer our economy through 	Page: 33 choppy waters today, and into unchartered territory tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have put in place many schemes to help our workers to get jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, there is friction in matching our unemployed to the job vacancies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Like Mr Patrick Tay has mentioned, the number of PMETs getting retrenched has increased.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is also getting harder to place them into the next jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, we need to expand options for our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Indeed, we need to up our game in employment facilitation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, I support the Minister's plan to work with best-in-class private placement companies to enhance our national employment facilitation capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I need to find out how the Ministry will work with the private placement companies to better facilitate employment facilitation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The larger and more enduring challenge, as highlighted by the Manpower Minister before, is in building a strong Singapore Core which can contribute to the overall Singapore workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Enforcement and guidance for Triple Weak companies are, indeed, necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And we need to also provide updates to the public on the outcomes of these enforcement actions so that not only is work done but also seen to be done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More important in building a Singapore Core is to ensure the paths to good jobs in thriving sectors remain open to our young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is important to note that "strong" need not always refer to numbers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Emerging or foreign businesses may require a larger foreign talent pool at the beginning due to local manpower constraints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, as the business matures, companies must increasingly localise its workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Its job profile should also reflect a Singapore Core.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially important in sectors that are growing and can provide job opportunities that are aligned with the aspirations of young Singaporeans, for example, in the information technology (IT) and finance sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One way in which we can build a stronger Singapore Core is to ensure that our graduates and mid-level professionals have a level playing field.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am not advocating overly protectionist and protective measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Being protectionist harms our long-term viability as a business hub.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, without further measures, our young Singaporeans and workers may find it challenging to enter Employment Pass-dominated sectors like the infocomm technology (ICT) or move up the ranks in that industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Foreign applicants usually have more job experience than our fresh graduates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Landing the job itself is an important first step for our locals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thereafter, committed company training and career pathways can help them anchor the core of a company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, certain high growth and critical sectors such as ICT, needs to be managed strategically.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, we know that there is no foreign worker quota for the Employment Pass (EP) category.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can highlight to companies that they need to not only grow their businesses but also commit to growing Singaporean talent.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Importantly, it allows our young Singaporeans to have a more level playing field to succeed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With 	Page: 34 this, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Madam, WDA has contributed a great deal to the upgrading of Singapore's workforce.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Now, in keeping with the changes in its role, it has been renamed to WSG.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Under the double whammy of economic restructuring and manpower shortage, local enterprises need to change their business mindsets and management models.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Some businessmen react fast and act swiftly and have already made their adjustments.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: But some others are still blinded to this reality, adhering to the notion of "there will be a way out once we reach the bottom of the mountain", and moving one step at a time, asking for help only when problems arise.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that WSG could find a way to communicate with these businessmen effectively, convincing them that a mindset change is necessary to counter the challenges of an ageing population, and to create more attractive employment opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: These are areas where high value-added industries and emerging industries have a distinct advantage.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, these industries cannot be assessed in terms of economic gain but their social contribution.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Methods used by some large corporations may not apply to traditional industries or SMEs.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: It gets even more problematic when the equipment become faulty and become intermittent pains of the overall restructuring process.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: During the restructuring process, SMEs realise that change is necessary, but may not have the means to implement the changes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: However, a crucial factor is how everyone could play a complementary role.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the battlefield, businessmen need weapons and ammunition.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: WDA needs to assist businessmen to upgrade their artillery and equipment, while the SSG should be responsible for manufacturing the bullets.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This shows that MOM and MOE have to work very closely together in order to reap real benefits for the business community.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are already experiencing evolving skills demand, given the rapid changes in both current and emerging jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister had mentioned, in order for WSG to be effective in its function of strengthening the Singaporean Core and promoting the development, competitiveness and employability of the Singapore workforce, WSG will have to work in close alignment with the proposed SSG in matching manpower supply with industry demand for both new entrants as well as the existing workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we discuss the functions for WSG, I would like to touch on three key phenomena that are impacting employment as well as organisational effectiveness and risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One, the impact of societal, geographical and technological changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Two, the "uberisation" of the workforce as described by John Bremen from Willis Towers Watson.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And third, the impact on women in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As highlighted in the World Economic Report 2016 on "The Future of Jobs, Employment, Skills and Workforce Strategy for the Fourth Industrial Revolution", demographics and societal trends, for example longevity and ageing societies, a growing middle class, flexible work arrangements, rapid urbanisation, women economic power and aspirations, concurrent with the technological revolution are already and will be expected to have a significant impact on jobs, ranging from a significant job creation to job displacement, and from heightened labour productivity to widening skills gaps.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because against the landscape of disruption to both employment and business models, businesses, too, will need to play an active role in developing talent regardless of the employment trends or they would be left with a talent gap and an inability to capitalise on the new opportunities emerging.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Page: 36 Even as WSG drives efforts to help Singaporeans assume quality jobs and careers, while addressing industry manpower needs, the employment landscape itself is changing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Models and platforms for how work is organised is changing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are already seeing an increasing use of contract workers and contingent staff by many companies, both large and small, for lower level and even PME roles, and the emergence of new platforms connecting skills to consumers who need their service.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This changes the relationship of companies with employees and also the face of the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This, in turn, if not managed effectively, will impact companies in the quality of their products and services, safety, customer experience and increased business cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While WSG works with businesses to structure and design jobs to fully tap the value of skills of each worker in order to enhance the quality of jobs and develop talent and improve sustainability, productivity and innovation, there is also a need to understand the needs and challenges faced by workers in a landscape of new and alternative work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the emerging employment trends, there will be a need to enable individuals to build and manage their careers as employees, as contract workers or even freelance or independent workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There is a need for policies to provide benefits and protection for the diverse work arrangements and how people work.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We have to start thinking of and separating worker benefits and protection from employment with a company.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This has larger implications not just for jobs but the job security and financial stability of the individual worker as well as economic and social stability with the growing income gap between those with relevant skills and those without.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The final point that I would like to touch on is that of the disproportionate negative impact on women.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Minister so aptly put it, the key is partnership.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the renaming as well as the revised and enhanced functions and powers of the WSG which complement those of the proposed SSG.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are, however, a few suggestions that I have which I hope MOM will consider in finalising the functions and powers of WSG.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I strongly support this, I would also urge the Ministry to focus not just on employment, reemployment and employability matters, but to consider including doing meaningful work post-retirement as part of WSG's initiatives.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, retired seniors can be trained and assisted to take up positions as healthcare case managers for other seniors who have chronic illnesses or other health conditions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These senior case managers are the ones to regularly and consistently visit the other seniors with chronic illnesses or health conditions to monitor their overall health, vital statistics, check on their diets and medications and whether they are following up with their doctors or healthcare providers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These senior case managers may not necessarily get a fixed monthly salary but may instead get allowances for transport, meals and time spent, very similar to our existing Pioneer Generation Ambassadors.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, retired seniors and stay-at-home mothers or fathers can also be trained to become community caregivers for the elderly or for young children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They can be the ones to provide some caregiving relief to full-time caregivers and support them in their work.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Similarly, they may not necessarily get a fixed monthly salary but instead allowances for transport, expenses and time spent.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our society ages and as our total fertility rate continue to remain low, we need a lot more social and community support from one another and we need to look at how such support can complement employment and employability for our people.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For clause 10, I am encouraged that more will be done to help our job seekers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They need help, largely because they still need to support young school-going children and elderly parents.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope WSG can help this group learn new skills and embrace the use of new and smart technologies that can help them in their jobs and careers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that having separate agencies with a more targeted focus will allow for more robust decision-making.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the amendments, which enables the new agency to play a more extensive role in helping job-seekers find and keep jobs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In clauses 9 and 10, increasing workforce productivity is clearly stated as a key objective for the agency.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this current climate of slower employment growth and economic uncertainties, it is important for the Government to focus our efforts on boosting productivity and to set up more safeguards than ever to protect our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Reiterating what Minister Lim Swee Say said in the Budget debates this year, we need a new breakthrough in productivity growth, or low economic growth will become the new norm, as our international competitiveness will be at risk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there have been strong efforts by the Government to increase automation to increase productivity, we must recognise that there are businesses for which there is no or little substitute for human workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, SMEs and companies in retail, hospitality, food and beverage and construction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Interestingly, it was mentioned earlier this year that it is precisely these same domestic sectors, such as retail and construction, which were the laggards in productivity growth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this regard, I commend efforts to look beyond automation to increase productivity to areas, such as job re-design, as stated in clauses 9(c) and 10(c), to render work more fulfilling and meaningful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should also focus our efforts on fostering innovation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Innovative economies tend to have higher productivity growth, measured by indices, such as the intensity of research and development (R&D), patent activity and entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore tends to do very well in both R&D and patent activity, but perhaps less well in entrepreneurship.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Young Singaporeans, relative to their peers in countries, such as the United States, still lack the tenacity and boldness to leap into the riskier field of entrepreneurship, where many unknowns lurk.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Without the necessary support, many potential Singaporean Mark Zuckerbergs would give up and too many brilliant ideas would go undiscovered.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: WSG will be in close contact with our workforce and companies, and while fostering a spirit of entrepreneurship is not the core focus of WSG, I hope that the two new agencies proposed to 	Page: 39 strengthen our workforce can also work with SPRING Singapore to look into how we can foster amongst our young a spirit of entrepreneurship, a generation daring enough to step out of their comfort zone and able to intuitively think out of the box.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I would like to raise a point regarding the link between workplace satisfaction and productivity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a 2016 survey, two of the top attributes employees look for were a "good work-life balance" and a "pleasant atmosphere" – both of which Singapore employers scored relatively poorly on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This was not unexpected, as almost half of our workforce reported that they were working more than the MOM's recommended limit of 44 working hours per week.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a survey conducted last year, three in 10 Singapore employees were thinking of resigning, citing reasons, such as poor leadership and disinterest in their job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Meanwhile, this problem also seems to plague newer entrants into the job market – the millennials – of whom a high seven in 10 said they were willing to move overseas for the right job.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a country lauded for its great wealth and top-class quality of life, Singapore's disenchanted workforce is perhaps the white elephant in the room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is something any new agency with a mandate to help our employees must take a serious look at.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To remain competitive, we need to ensure that our workforce is not one which is simply productive, but also fulfilled and serve their roles with enthusiasm with collective achievement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are many high-profile cases where a happy workforce can transform a company, and this can be applied to Singapore's economy.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As SkillsFuture gets its own agency, WDA will be renamed WSG and focuses on employment and workplace practices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Research has shown that flexi-work can increase productivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In one study, call-centre workers increased their productivity by 13% when they were allowed to work from home and that is just short-term productivity.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Long-term productivity probably increases as well, as workers feel happier, can balance their personal lives and are less likely to quit.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Flexi-work can benefit our society in other ways, too.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Workers can find more time to pursue lifelong learning or have kids.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Many people have told me that they cannot make it to their children's childcare centre on time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Just last night during my MPS, a resident came and spoke to me.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She said that she has to reach the childcare centre by 6.00 pm in Yishun and she works in town and, for every minute that 	Page: 40 she is late, she will have to pay $5.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And if they can work from home, then they can work the same amount of time and still make it to their children's childcare centre.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just about working from home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I have a friend who lives in the United Kingdom (UK) and he recently came to Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He and his wife have a three-year-old daughter and they take turns to pick their daughter up from the childcare centre.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said that on the days that he has to pick up his daughter, he will go into office two hours earlier and he will leave two hours earlier.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, in fact, the childcare centre, according to him, closes at 4.00 pm, but they have no problems in bringing their daughter home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, if we can have similar flexi-hours, I am sure many of our residents will be happier to have more babies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many percent of our companies can allow this?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But if we look deeper into the survey, most of the flexible arrangements offered were part-time work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It often means less pay, lower bonuses and no promotions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Less than 10% offer staggered hours and permanent working from home arrangements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If we want to harness the benefits of flexi-work, then these numbers need to go up by quite a lot.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, companies offering certain options do not mean employees will take them up.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This could be due to the culture of "face time" in local companies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But our gross domestic product is not 50% more than theirs!

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This shows that we are not as productive during office hours.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I urge employers to make their culture friendlier to flexi-work, and employees to boldly ask for flexi-work arrangements they need.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some countries have laws that say employees cannot be penalised for asking for flexi-work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that the Government has provided more grants to employers who introduce flexi-work and I look forward to the positive results.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   A survey revealed that companies that allow workers to have flexi working hours and to work long-term from home account for less than 15%.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: If this ratio can be increased, I believe that it will increase our productivity and also enable our people to enjoy better work-life balance and thereby encourage more people to join the workforce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government has already increased the grants to companies which have flexi-work arrangements.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Moreover, we should also encourage employees to actively approach the employers to discuss flexi-work arrangements so that they do not have to resign.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As I have said earlier, I have a friend who lives in the UK and came to Singapore recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He and his wife have an adorable three-year-old daughter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said he and his wife have to pick up their daughter from the childcare centre on time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: When it is my friend's turn to pick up his daughter, he would go to office two hours earlier so that he can leave the office two hours earlier 	Page: 41 to pick up his daughter.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: He said that this is a very common practice in the UK.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We hope that such practices can also become common in Singapore and hopefully, it can encourage Singaporeans to have more children.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In English): Madam, I support this Bill and hope WSG will further promote all types of flexible working arrangements.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As I have mentioned earlier, we are cognisant of the issues faced by PMETs, especially those mid-career, in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are going to customise PCP sector by sector because the issues involved in professional conversion vary across sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In the case of CSP, I agree with Mr Patrick Tay that we ought to find ways to create greater awareness.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I assure the Member that we are working on some breakthrough ideas so that CSP will become more widespread, not just among the employees, but also the employers as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, I also want to emphasise one point again as we extend additional support to PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: WSG will do its very best, but no matter how much it does, on its own, will not be enough.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, in the case of NTUC, the U PME Centre is doing a great job under the leadership of Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I hope that WSG can, likewise, extend our partnerships with U PME Centre and all the other partners as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Desmond Choo suggested that we should strengthen public-private partnerships in job placements for PMETs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We studied the experience of Australia and the UK.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We concluded that with the right design and incentive structure, it is possible to encourage employment agencies to be more jobseeker-centric, rather than client-centric.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are now working very actively with the industry and we intend to partner some of these "best in class" employment agencies.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Soon, you will hear some of our new initiatives in this area.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Jessica Tan spoke about the impact of disruptive change at the workplace on workers, all sorts of workers, especially for women.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In fact, we share the same concerns about job creation as well as job disruption.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: This is the reason why we are going to pay greater attention to not just a traditional work arrangement, but emerging work arrangements as well mentioned by Ms Jessica Tan – freelancing, contract workers, and independent workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Page: 42 Ms Jessica Tan may be happy to hear that WDA, or the soon-to-be WSG, has formed partnerships with associations and the NTUC to reach out to the freelancing sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We even customise our PCP for the freelancers working in the creative industries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I also want to assure Ms Jessica Tan that we will be working very closely with SSG to match skills with job and employment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Employment and employability – the two will have to go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In terms of support for the industry and, in particular, for SMEs, as highlighted by Mr Thomas Chua and Mr Louis Ng, again, we share their views completely.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Thomas Chua highlighted a very important point.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As SMEs go through a process of restructuring, the kind of support they need is quite holistic – manpower, technology, funding support and, most importantly, ideas on how to transform their businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Under the LED scheme, all the Government agencies have come together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We started the LED scheme in October last year and, since then, all the agencies, including SPRING, Infocomm Development Agency (IDA), WDA and NTUC e2i, are all working together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are now providing a one-stop service to all SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I am also very happy to say that SMEs are also beginning to come together.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, just last week or two weeks ago, we worked with about 10 Indian restaurants.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many of them have restaurants in Little India.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: During one meeting with them, they told me that many of the Indian restaurants in Little India may have to close down, and I said, "If that happens, that will be a national disaster".

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I asked them what is the problem and they told me that the problem was manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They are not able to attract enough locals to join the sector, for example, to become a local chef trained in Indian cuisine.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, due to the manpower quota limitations, they are not able to hire enough foreign workers to meet their requirements.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: After working together for about one year now, finally, we have achieved a breakthrough.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What they did was – as mentioned by Mr Thomas Chua – individually, they are not able to invest in the technology, mechanisation and automation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Each piece of equipment costs from $20,000 to as high as $200,000, and there is no way each of these restaurants could make that kind of investment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: What is even more exciting is that at this central kitchen, we will also be training local chefs so that in time to come, the Singaporean Core in these Indian restaurants and sector will be strengthened as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe that if we are able to get more and more SMEs to come together, not individually, but collectively, we can speed up the process of not just mechanisation, but innovation breakthrough, as mentioned by Mr Thomas Chua as well as Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah highlighted the impact of the future workplace on women.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If you look at the labour force participation rate and the employment rate, these are high in Singapore by global standards.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But compared to the rate for males, there is still room for further strengthening.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, there is still a lot of scope for us to work together to tap more on our women workforce, as highlighted by both hon Members.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Page: 43 The tripartite partners have been working very closely together to make our workplace family-friendly.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We are making very promising and very steady progress but obviously, there is a lot more that can be done.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We will take up the suggestions by Ms Jessica Tan and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah to see how we can push this forward.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Louis Ng asked what kind of additional support we can give to sectors and businesses where the human interaction cannot be mechanised.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In other words, some sectors focus more on high-touch.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: With high-touch, does it mean that there is no scope for us to introduce technology?

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We believe that high-touch and high-tech both can go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have helped some businesses to be more high-tech and, as a result, we free up the manpower to focus on high-touch services.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Many of the workers spend a lot of their time doing stock-taking.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, they are now able to do their stock-taking within minutes, at the most, hours.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: You just use the RFID reader, do a scan in the shop, within minutes, the stocktaking is done.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As a result, the workers are now being retrained to spend more time not on stocktaking, but serving customers, doing upselling and so on.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, I think the two can go hand in hand.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: On the foreign worker issue, Mr Desmond Choo asked whether we can implement a quota for EP holders, particularly in the high growth sectors like IT.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In many sectors, we just do not have the number, whether it is engineers in the wafer fab or sales staff in the retail sector.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we need the foreign manpower to complement the shortage and bridge the number gap.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In Singapore, our workforce is a good one but we cannot claim to have all the expertise that we need, especially in new growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: For example, with SkillsFuture, we can speed up the training and upgrading of manpower to meet our future needs.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, we need foreign manpower to meet our numbers gap, the skills gap and the timing gap.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The extent of the gaps varies across sectors.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Some sectors face greater challenges in skilsl gap, whereas some sectors may face more of a numbers gap issue.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Also, as each individual sector goes through the process of development, at various stages of development, again, they have different challenges.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: In bioscience today, our manpower expertise gap is a lot greater compared to sectors which are more mature.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And as a result, if we try to impose a quota on EPs across all the sectors, even for selective sectors, I think it will be very difficult for us to strike the right balance.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we impose it too tightly, it will stifle the growth of our economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: If we make it too loose, then, it will offer no protection for our local workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Therefore, what we have been doing, and I think it is the right thing to do, is to be smarter in the way we make use of the foreign manpower by maximising the complementarity between the 	Page: 44 foreign manpower and the local manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: At the same time, we encourage more of them to become "triple strong" so that we will see not just a stronger Singaporean Core, but also the transfer of know-how to strengthen the complementarity between the foreign workforce and the local workforce.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I want to assure Mr Desmond Choo that our determination to strengthen the Singaporean Core is a real one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We have already taken action and we will continue to push for that.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested that WSG conduct research into underemployment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I believe this is one area brought up by Ms Sylvia Lim during the COS as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: MOM is equally concerned about whether there is underlying growth in under-employment, not just time-based but also in terms of actual utilisation of the full potential of manpower.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I will take the Member's suggestion into account when we formulate the WSG's research agenda.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar suggested that we should provide retirees and stay-at-home parents with meaningful work such as caregiving in the community.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: I support her idea, and I believe that the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and the Ministry of Health (MOH) are already working on this, and WSG will certainly support the various Ministries.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: As we go through this transition, human resource has to be viewed as our human capital.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Human resource is not just a number, a person for you to use, but it is for us to invest in.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: The more we invest in human resource, the more valuable this human capital will be in our future economy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They use terms like rapid innovation, smart innovation, pervasive innovation.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, we are not the only country or economy that is trying to run fast.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: They, too, are trying to run fast with innovation, with technology.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And yet, at the same time, they all recognise that this innovation-driven growth must also be an inclusive one.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Otherwise, they will not be able to solve their problem with high youth unemployment and sticky unemployment.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: We, in Singapore, I think this is an area we have done better than them for many years.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: And this is the reason why in Singapore our economic growth has been healthy.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: But more importantly, we have been able to create enough good and meaningful jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Page: 45 Moving forward, the same challenge remains.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: Yes, we must move fast to make every job a better job, move fast to make every worker a better worker but, most importantly, let us make sure that we progress in sync between these two to ensure that every better job will be able to find a better worker and every better worker will be able to find a better job.

speaker: Mr Lim Swee Say
text: So, with that, we, hopefully, will be able to arrive at a state whereby every career in Singapore can be a better career for all Singaporeans.
